1.4.1.examLens: Know the five principles in order, who defines value, and the Japanese vocabulary. These are mostly recall points.

worked.question: A team notices that invoices wait in a pile until 50 have accumulated, then are processed together. Name the Lean concepts at work and say what the fix is.
worked.solution: It is batching (and a push system), which creates waiting and delays defect discovery. The fix is one-piece flow and a pull signal, so each invoice moves as soon as the previous step finishes.

1.4.2.examLens: Matching questions: who developed what, and which came first.

worked.question:
Match: (1) jidoka, (2) SMED, (3) Lean Thinking, (4) moving assembly line.
(A) Womack and Jones (B) Sakichi Toyoda (C) Henry Ford (D) Shigeo Shingo

1.4.3.examLens: Choose the right approach from the symptoms in a scenario.

worked.question: A bakery's cakes come out the right size only 70% of the time, but each order is ready on schedule. A second bakery has consistent cakes, but orders take three days because trays wait for ovens. Which approach does each need most?
worked.solution: First bakery: Six Sigma (variation and defects, with no delay problem). Second bakery: Lean (waiting and flow, with no defect problem).

1.4.4.examLens: Classify a situation into the right waste. IASSC uses its own names, which differ from the popular TIMWOOD list, so learn both.

worked.question: Classify each: (a) a technician walks 40 meters to a tool cabinet several times per shift; (b) a report is sent to five managers for approval when two would do; (c) 200 units sit between assembly and test; (d) a batch is scrapped and remade.

1.4.5.examLens: Name the five S's in order and identify which S an action represents.

worked.question: Which S is each? (a) Removing 30 broken fixtures nobody uses. (b) Painting outlines on the wall for each tool. (c) Writing a one-page standard for how the cell is laid out. (d) The area's 5S slipped after three months; the manager starts weekly audits.

1.4.1.a.title: The five Lean principles
1.4.1.a.html:
From Womack and Jones, in order:

  1. Specify value from the customer's point of view.
  2. Map the value stream: every step from raw material to customer.
  3. Create flow: remove interruptions so work moves without stopping.
  4. Establish pull: produce only what the next step or customer asks for.
  5. Pursue perfection: keep improving; the process is never finished.

1.4.1.b.title: Value is defined by the customer
1.4.1.b.html: Not by the company, the department, or the engineer. If the customer would not pay for a step, it is not value, however hard people work at it.

1.4.1.c.title: VA, NVA, and necessary NVA
1.4.1.c.html:
• Value-added: the customer would pay for it.
  • Non-value-added: the customer would not pay for it. Remove it.
  • Necessary non-value-added: required by law, policy, or current technology, so it cannot be dropped today, but it should be minimized.

In most processes, value-added time is only a small share of the total lead time (see process cycle efficiency in 1.2.5.h).

1.4.1.d.title: Push versus pull, flow versus batch
1.4.1.d.html:
• Push: work is produced on a schedule or forecast and pushed to the next step whether or not it is ready. Inventory piles up.
  • Pull: a step produces only when the next step signals it needs more (kanban is the classic signal).
  • Batch: work moves in groups. Items wait for the rest of the batch, and defects hide until the whole batch is checked.
  • One-piece flow: work moves one unit at a time. Defects are caught immediately, and lead time falls.

Example: a clerk processes 100 forms before passing them on. If the first form had an error, all 100 may contain it. Passing forms one at a time exposes the error after the first.

1.4.1.e.title: Muda, Mura, Muri
1.4.1.e.html:
• Muda: waste (activity that adds cost but no value).
  • Mura: unevenness (irregular workload, so people are rushed one day and idle the next).
  • Muri: overburden (pushing people or machines beyond what they can sustain).

Mura and Muri often cause Muda.

1.4.1.f.title: Lean vocabulary (recall only)
1.4.1.f.html:
• Takt time: available time ÷ customer demand; the pace of the customer.
  • Kaizen: continuous, incremental improvement by everyone.
  • Gemba: the place where the work happens; go there to see the facts.
  • SMED: single-minute exchange of dies, meaning fast changeover between products.
  • TPM: total productive maintenance; operators help keep equipment running.
  • Jidoka: automation with a human touch; the process stops when it detects a defect.
  • Heijunka: level scheduling; smooths volume and mix to reduce Mura.
  • Andon: a visual or audible alert that signals a problem.
  • Standard work: the documented, best-known way to do the job.
  • One-piece flow: moving work one unit at a time.

1.4.1.g.title: The two pillars
1.4.1.g.html: Lean rests on respect for people and continuous improvement. Workers who do the job are expected to find and fix the waste.

1.4.2.a.title: Toyota's founders and engineers
1.4.2.a.html:
• Sakichi Toyoda built looms that stop automatically when a thread breaks. That idea became jidoka.
  • Taiichi Ohno built the Toyota Production System (TPS) after World War II.
  • Shigeo Shingo contributed SMED (fast changeover) and poka-yoke (mistake-proofing).

1.4.2.b.title: Just-in-time and pull
1.4.2.b.html: Just-in-time means making only what is needed, when it is needed, in the amount needed. It grew out of Kiichiro Toyoda's idea and became the basis of pull production and kanban.

1.4.2.c.title: Ford's flow line
1.4.2.c.html: Henry Ford's moving assembly line (Highland Park, 1913) was an early example of continuous flow. It was efficient for a single product, but it had little variety, which Toyota later addressed.

1.4.2.d.title: The word "Lean"
1.4.2.d.html: The term "lean" was popularized by researcher John Krafcik in the late 1980s. James Womack, Daniel Jones, and Daniel Roos wrote The Machine That Changed the World (1990) about the auto industry. Womack and Jones followed with Lean Thinking (1996), which set out the five principles.

1.4.2.e.title: Who developed what
1.4.2.e.html: If the question names a concept, pull out the one-line link in the table above. If it asks for order: Sakichi Toyoda and Ford (early 1900s), then Ohno and the TPS (post-war), then the term "Lean" (1980s to 1990).

1.4.3.a.title: What each attacks
1.4.3.a.html:
• Lean attacks waste, flow, and lead time.
  • Six Sigma attacks variation and defects.

1.4.3.b.title: Complementary, not competing
1.4.3.b.html: Both are customer-focused and data-driven. A process that is fast but inconsistent needs Six Sigma. One that is consistent but slow and wasteful needs Lean. Lean Six Sigma combines them: fast and right.

1.4.3.c.title: When to use which
1.4.3.c.html:
SymptomLeanSix Sigma
Long lead time, lots of waiting✔
Excess inventory, extra handling✔
Defects, rework, inconsistent results✔
Output varies widely between runs or shifts✔
Both slow and error-prone✔✔

1.4.3.d.title: Lean tools sit inside DMAIC
1.4.3.d.html:
You do not choose between Lean and DMAIC. Lean tools are used within the phases:

  • Define/Measure: value stream map, process mapping, waste identification.
  • Analyze: waste analysis, process cycle efficiency.
  • Improve: 5S, kanban, one-piece flow, poka-yoke.
  • Control: visual management, standard work, audits.

1.4.3.e.title: Which approach fits
1.4.3.e.html: Look for the language in the scenario. "Waiting," "backlog," "queue," and "inventory" point to Lean. "Defects," "variation," "inconsistent," and "out of spec" point to Six Sigma.

1.4.4.a.title: IASSC wording
1.4.4.a.html:
The seven wastes: Overproduction, Correction, Inventory, Motion, Overprocessing, Conveyance, Waiting.

  • Overproduction: making more, or sooner, than the customer needs.
  • Correction: fixing defects (rework, repair, scrap).
  • Inventory: more material or work-in-process than needed.
  • Motion: unnecessary movement by people (reaching, walking, searching).
  • Overprocessing: doing more work than the customer values (extra approvals, tighter tolerance than required).
  • Conveyance: unnecessary movement of materials or information between places.
  • Waiting: idle time waiting for the next step.

1.4.4.b.title: Cross-walk to TIMWOOD
1.4.4.b.html:
TIMWOOD stands for Transportation, Inventory, Motion, Waiting, Overproduction, Overprocessing, Defects. The two names that differ are:

  • Correction = Defects
  • Conveyance = Transportation

Everything else matches.

1.4.4.c.title: Overproduction
1.4.4.c.html: Overproduction is often called the worst waste, because it creates the others: extra inventory, extra handling, extra storage, and more chances for defects.

1.4.4.d.title: The eighth waste
1.4.4.d.html: Many sources add an eighth: unused talent, meaning not using people's knowledge, skills, and ideas.

1.4.4.e.title: Classify the example
1.4.4.e.html:
• Excess WIP piled between steps = inventory.
  • Walking across the plant to retrieve tools = motion.
  • Entering the same data into two systems = overprocessing.
  • Reworking a scratched part = correction.
  • Forklift moving parts between buildings = conveyance.
  • Operators idle while waiting for material = waiting.
  • Producing 500 units when 300 were ordered = overproduction.

1.4.4.f.title: Overprocessing versus correction
1.4.4.f.html:
• Overprocessing: doing more than the customer needs, even when everything goes right.
  • Correction: doing work again because something went wrong.

A polishing step that customers do not notice is overprocessing. Re-polishing a part that came out scratched is correction.

1.4.5.a.title: The five S's
1.4.5.a.html:
1. Sort (Seiri)
  2. Straighten (Seiton), also called Set in order
  3. Shine (Seiso)
  4. Standardize (Seiketsu)
  5. Self-Discipline (Shitsuke), also called Sustain

IASSC uses the term Self-Discipline for the fifth.

1.4.5.b.title: What each one means
1.4.5.b.html:
• Sort: remove what is not needed. Items of doubt get a red tag and are moved to a holding area.
  • Straighten: a place for everything and everything in its place (shadow boards, labels, marked locations).
  • Shine: clean the area and inspect equipment while cleaning. Cleaning reveals leaks, wear, and problems.
  • Standardize: set rules and visual standards so everyone does it the same way.
  • Self-Discipline: make it a habit through training, audits, and leadership.

1.4.5.c.title: The sixth S
1.4.5.c.html: Extension. Some organizations add Safety as a sixth S. The official wording lists five.

1.4.5.d.title: Visual management
1.4.5.d.html: Make the status of the work visible at a glance: floor markings, shadow boards, color coding, labels, and andon boards. Anyone walking in should see immediately what is normal and what is not.

1.4.5.e.title: Identify which S
1.4.5.e.html:
• Red-tag area = Sort.
  • Shadow board = Straighten.
  • Daily cleaning with an inspection checklist = Shine.
  • Color-coded standard layouts and posted rules = Standardize.
  • Regular audits and habit-building = Self-Discipline.

1.4.1-1.stem: In the five Lean principles, which one comes immediately after "map the value stream"?
1.4.1-1.explanation: The order is specify value, map the value stream, create flow, establish pull, pursue perfection.

1.4.1-2.stem: A step produces more only when the next step sends back an empty container. Which type of system is this?
1.4.1-2.explanation: Work is triggered by a downstream signal, which is pull.

1.4.1-3.stem: Workload swings between overloaded days and idle days. Which Lean term describes this?
1.4.1-3.explanation: Mura is unevenness. Muda is waste and Muri is overburden.

1.4.1-4.stem: A machine stops automatically when it detects a defective part. Which Lean term describes this?
1.4.1-4.explanation: Jidoka is automation that stops on a defect. Andon is the visual or audible alert, heijunka is level scheduling, and gemba is where the work happens.

1.4.1-5.stem: In Lean, value is defined by the company's engineers.

1.4.2-2.stem: Which 1996 book set out the five Lean principles?

options.html: The Machine That Changed the World

1.4.2-2.explanation: Lean Thinking by Womack and Jones (1996). The Machine That Changed the World (1990) was about the auto industry.

1.4.2-3.stem: Which early example of continuous flow production is considered a precursor of Lean?
1.4.2-3.explanation: Ford's moving assembly line (1913) demonstrated continuous flow, though with little product variety.

1.4.3-1.stem: Shipments are accurate, but the average lead time is 9 days because orders wait between steps. Which approach fits best?
1.4.3-1.explanation: Waiting and long lead time are flow and waste problems, which is Lean territory.

1.4.3-2.stem: Output varies widely from shift to shift, and 12% of units fail inspection. Which focus fits best?

options.html: Six Sigma, to reduce variation and defects

1.4.3-2.explanation: Inconsistent output and defects point to variation, which Six Sigma attacks.

1.4.3-3.stem: Which Lean tools are most likely to be used in the Control phase?

options.html: A Pareto chart of defect types

1.4.3-3.explanation: Control holds the gains with visual management, standard work, and audits.

1.4.4-1.stem: Operators walk 40 meters several times per shift to fetch a tool. Which waste is this?
1.4.4-1.explanation: Unnecessary movement by people is motion. Conveyance is the movement of materials.

1.4.4-2.stem: A forklift moves parts between two buildings several times a day. Which waste is this?
1.4.4-2.explanation: Moving materials or information between places is conveyance.

1.4.4-3.stem: A part is polished to a finish the customer never requested and never sees. Which waste is this?
1.4.4-3.explanation: Doing more work than the customer values, even when everything goes right, is overprocessing. Correction is redoing work because something went wrong.

1.4.4-4.stem: Which IASSC waste name corresponds to "Defects" in the TIMWOOD list?
1.4.4-4.explanation: IASSC uses Correction for defects and Conveyance for transportation.

1.4.4-5.stem: Overproduction is often called the worst waste because it creates the other wastes.
1.4.4-5.explanation: Making more than is needed creates extra inventory, handling, storage, and opportunities for defects.

1.4.5-1.stem: A team paints an outline on a board for each tool. Which S is this?
1.4.5-1.explanation: A place for everything, such as shadow boards and labels, is Straighten.

1.4.5-2.stem: Which S is about habit, training, and audits that keep the other four going?
1.4.5-2.explanation: Self-Discipline (Sustain) turns the first four S's into a habit.

1.4.5-3.stem: Which TWO are among the five S's?
1.4.5-3.explanation: The five S's are Sort, Straighten, Shine, Standardize, and Self-Discipline.

1.4.5-4.stem: A team tags unneeded items and moves them to a holding area. Which S is this?
